name: Retrofuturism
visualIdentity: Explicitly, choose one historical period’s vision of the future and align objects, instruments, interfaces, typography, color, and motion to it. Analog controls, early computers, and space-age forms are examples; neon grids are not the sole direction.
suitableUses: Explicit fits include product or editorial introductions, explainers, illustrated narratives, and cinematic sequences. Interactive museum or brand experiences with operable period controls are an inferred fit; use only when the topic benefits from a coherent era and clear story.
limitations: One era should define the world; avoid mixing incompatible period templates, such as 1950s chrome with 1980s neon. Chaptered motion can be omitted for short topics or where transitions obscure causality, continuity, or a required loop. No canonical palette is specified.
palette: Palette is reference dependent. Optional example tokens: background cream #EEE3CB, foreground #314449, teal accent #6B9693, orange accent #BC7751. These are suggestions, not intrinsic colors; exact task, brand, or reference colors and role assignments take precedence. Keep accents subordinate, use discrete colors (no gradient), and place normal text on a verified readable backing; example foreground on cream is 8.027:1, but contrast must be checked on actual composites.
motionAndInteraction: Match movement to the chosen era’s mechanical and display language. Use authored, seekable, deterministic time; preserve deliberate cuts, impacts, and reading holds. Optional chapter handoffs and story steps coordinate copy and visuals; forward, backward, and direct seeking must resolve consistently. For interactive HTML, finite scroll progress can drive states; provide keyboard/touch access, readable static or reduced-motion states, and meaningful controls. These interactions are suitability guidance, not mandatory style traits.
audio: Unspecified by the style. Choose music, voice, effects, ambience, or silence for the subject and objective; honor supplied requirements and assets. Do not assume a genre or mandatory layer. Synchronize and mix separately, preserve speech clarity, and check clipping and picture sync.
assetRequirements: No fixed assets are specified. Build or source era-consistent objects, instruments, interfaces, type, and any 3D environment; use SVG for scalable interface layers and Three.js when dimensional geometry is needed. Load local fonts/assets and cache or deterministically replay stateful simulations. Distinguish simulated appearance from photographed production.
combinations: Retrofuturism alone can define the world. Optional style-075 supports operable analog controls with matching visible state changes and accessible HTML sliders/switches. Optional style-009 supports 1950s–60s typography and flat illustrated shapes behind dimensional objects. Keep supporting elements within the same period; avoid decorative, nonfunctional dials and brand pastiche.
productionApproach: Select renderer and motion method for fidelity and action: Three.js/SVG and GSAP are recommended; Motion is optional and must be explicitly synchronized. HyperFrames is the primary video assembly, timing, audio, validation, and export pipeline; Remotion is only a documented fallback when unavailable or unable to meet a verified requirement. Neither dictates visual design. Use seekable time, inspect representative states and final output. For HTML, keep live scroll/pointer behavior separate from video timing.
